title: Keys in lists
body: Why does React need a stable `key` prop on list items?

options.t: So reconciliation can match items between renders and preserve their state and DOM nodes

explanation: Use stable ids from your data. Array indexes as keys break when items are inserted, removed or reordered — state (e.g. input values) ends up attached to the wrong item.

title: Props vs state

options.t: Props are inputs passed by the parent and read-only for the child; state is owned and updated by the component
State is shared by all components automatically

answer: Props flow down and are read-only; state is local and updated via setters.
explanation: Lift state up to the closest common ancestor when siblings need it, or use context/a store for widely shared state.

title: Rules of Hooks
body: Which is a rule of Hooks?

options.t: Hooks may be called inside loops
Call Hooks only at the top level of React function components or custom Hooks, never conditionally
Hooks must be called inside class components
Each Hook can be used only once per app

answer: Top level only, same order every render.
explanation: React identifies hook state by call order. A conditional hook shifts the order and corrupts state; the eslint-plugin-react-hooks rules enforce this.

title: useEffect with an empty dependency array

options.t: After the first render (mount); cleanup runs on unmount

answer: Once after mount, cleanup on unmount.
explanation: In development StrictMode, React mounts, unmounts and remounts components once to surface missing cleanup, so effects run twice. Effects run after paint; use useLayoutEffect for synchronous DOM measurement.

title: Batched state updates
body: Starting from 0, what is `count` after one click?
explanation: All three calls read the same `count` (0) from this render's closure, so each schedules `setCount(1)`; React batches them. Use the updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)` to apply each update to the latest value (result 3).

title: useMemo vs useCallback

options.t: The function instance itself, keeping its identity stable between renders

explanation: `useCallback(fn, deps)` equals `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. It matters when passing callbacks to memoised children or using them as effect dependencies; otherwise it adds overhead without benefit.

title: useRef

options.t: Holding a mutable value that persists across renders without causing re-renders (and referencing DOM nodes)

answer: Persistent mutable box, no re-render on change.
explanation: Examples: DOM refs for focus, storing interval ids, keeping the latest value for callbacks. Don't read refs during render to compute output.

title: Stale closures in effects
body: An interval created in `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => console.log(count), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, [])` always logs 0. Why?

options.t: The callback closed over `count` from the first render; the effect never re-runs. Use a functional update, a ref, or add count to the dependencies

answer: Stale closure over the initial render's state.
explanation: Each render has its own props/state snapshot. Keep dependency arrays honest; for intervals updating state, `setCount(c => c + 1)` avoids needing `count` in the closure.

title: Redux reducers
body: Which is a requirement for a Redux reducer?

options.t: It must be a pure function that computes new state from the previous state and an action without mutating it

answer: Pure, no side effects, no mutation.
explanation: Redux Toolkit's `createSlice` lets you write 'mutating' code because Immer produces immutable updates under the hood. Side effects belong in thunks, listeners or RTK Query.

title: Context and re-renders
body: What happens when a Context provider's `value` changes?

options.t: Every component that consumes that context re-renders

explanation: Passing a new object literal each render (`value={{ user, setUser }}`) re-renders consumers every time; memoise the value, split contexts by update frequency, or use a store with selectors for high-frequency state.

title: Link vs anchor
body: Why use React Router's `<Link>` instead of `<a href>` for internal navigation?

options.t: It performs client-side navigation via the History API without a full page reload
Anchors are not allowed in React

explanation: A full reload loses in-memory state and re-downloads the app. `<NavLink>` adds active styling.

title: Reading route parameters
body: With the route `/users/:userId`, how does a component read `userId`?
explanation: `useSearchParams` reads query strings, `useNavigate` navigates programmatically, and data routers offer loaders/actions for route-level data fetching.

title: React.memo
body: What does wrapping a component in `React.memo` do?

options.t: Skips re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal to the previous props

explanation: It only helps if props are referentially stable — combine with useMemo/useCallback for object and function props, and measure with the React Profiler before optimising.

title: Rendering very large lists
body: A page must display 20,000 rows smoothly. What is the most effective technique?

options.t: Wrap each row in React.memo only
Virtualisation/windowing: render only the rows visible in the viewport (e.g. react-window)

explanation: Windowing keeps the DOM small regardless of data size. Combine with pagination or infinite loading for data fetching.

title: Controlled components
body: What makes an `<input>` a controlled component?

options.t: Its value is driven by React state via the value prop and updated through onChange

options.e: Reading values via refs is the uncontrolled approach.

answer: React state is the single source of truth for its value.
explanation: Controlled inputs enable instant validation and formatting; uncontrolled inputs (refs/defaultValue) can be simpler for large forms; libraries like React Hook Form mix both.

title: How React updates the UI
body: Explain what happens when state changes in a React component, from the state update to the DOM change.
answer: React schedules a re-render, calls the component to produce new elements, reconciles them against the previous tree, and commits only the differences to the DOM.
explanation:
1. `setState` schedules an update (batched).
2. **Render phase:** React calls the component (and children not bailed out) to get a new element tree — pure computation.
3. **Reconciliation:** it diffs new vs previous elements by type and key; same type keeps the instance and state, different type remounts.
4. **Commit phase:** it applies the minimal DOM mutations, then runs layout effects and, after paint, passive effects (useEffect).
With concurrent rendering, the render phase can be interrupted for urgent updates.
reference: State updates are batched and schedule a render; React re-invokes components to produce a new element tree, reconciles it with the previous tree using element type and keys, then commits minimal DOM changes and runs effects. Rendering is pure and may be interrupted in concurrent mode; commits are synchronous.
